blocks.text: Jeremiah speaks at the temple gate to people arriving to worship, but the chapter rejects the idea that the temple itself guarantees their safety. Remaining in the land is linked instead to changed conduct: justice between neighbors, protection for the sojourner, orphan, and widow, and the rejection of violence and other gods. The accusations that follow show why worship cannot be separated from conduct: theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, idolatry, and the practices at Topheth contradict the security the people claim when they stand in the house called by Jehovah’s name.

The phrase “den of robbers” in verse 11 has figured in a disputed interpretation of a fig-tree intercalation and temple action. In that reading, those scenes address Jerusalem’s leadership and questions of the temple’s fruit, prayer, nations, commerce, and judgment. This interpretation should not be used to foster contempt for Judaism or for sacred places.

The received book of Jeremiah contains poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix. A practical outline places chapter 7 within chapters 2–25, while questions about the book’s long compositional and textual history remain disputed.
